why_how.text: The Safety Responsibility Act makes drivers answerable for the harm they cause, and liability insurance is how most drivers meet that duty.
Carrying and showing proof lets officers and crash victims confirm a driver can pay for harm caused.

scenario.text: Nina causes a crash that injures two people and damages a fence.

reasoning.text: Her liability minimums are sixty thousand dollars for injury to two or more people and twenty-five thousand for property.

result.text: Her policy must provide at least sixty thousand dollars for the two injured people and twenty-five thousand for the fence.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking one single minimum amount covers every kind of crash harm.

correction.text: The minimums split three ways: thirty thousand for one person, sixty thousand for two or more, and twenty-five thousand for property.

prompt.text: A driver injures one pedestrian in a crash. What minimum liability coverage applies to that injury?

rationale.text: The one-person minimum is thirty thousand dollars; sixty thousand applies to two or more people, and twenty-five thousand to property.

title.text: Paying for the harm you cause

narration.text: This lesson opens the section on safety responsibility. Driving comes with a financial duty. If you cause a crash, you are expected to pay for the injuries and damage you cause, and Texas law makes sure drivers can. We will look at the Safety Responsibility Act, the three minimum liability amounts every policy must meet, and the occasions when you must show proof of insurance, both routine visits and on-demand requests. These amounts are among the most tested numbers in this section, so we will spend time keeping them apart and tying each one to the right kind of harm.

The Texas Motor Vehicle Safety Responsibility Act makes every owner and every operator of a motor vehicle financially answerable for death, injury, or property damage they cause. To meet that duty, drivers must carry at least minimum liability insurance. Notice that the rule reaches both owners and operators, so borrowing a car does not move the duty away from the person driving. The Act is the reason insurance proof shows up at so many steps in this handbook, from licensing to registration to inspection, and it underpins every penalty you will see later in this section.

lines.text: Sixty thousand: two or more people.

narration.text: Minimum liability coverage in Texas has three parts. A policy must cover at least thirty thousand dollars for injury or death of one person, at least sixty thousand dollars for injury or death of two or more people in the same crash, and at least twenty-five thousand dollars for property damage. Think of it as one person, more people, and things. Many drivers carry more than these amounts, but these are the minimums every policy must meet. When a question asks about a minimum, first decide whether the harm was to one person, to several people, or to property.

lines.text: Show proof at licensing, registration, inspection.
Hand proof to officers and crash parties.

narration.text: Every driver must keep liability insurance or qualify as self-insured, unless exempt. You show proof routinely when you apply for a license, register a vehicle, or have it inspected. You also hand proof to any police officer who asks and to any person involved in a crash with you. So there are two kinds of occasions. Routine occasions are the office visits you plan for, while on-demand occasions come up on the road whenever an officer or another driver in a crash requests it. Keep your proof with you, so you are ready for both kinds of occasion.

Here is a trap built from three close numbers. The minimum amounts are easy to swap, especially sixty thousand and twenty-five thousand. Thirty thousand dollars is the minimum for injury or death of one person. Sixty thousand is the minimum when two or more people are hurt or killed. Twenty-five thousand is the minimum for property damage, such as another car or a fence. A question might describe a crash that hurts one person and damages a car. Then two minimums apply at once: thirty thousand for the person and twenty-five thousand for the car.

Here is a quick check: a driver injures one pedestrian in a crash. What minimum liability coverage applies to that injury? Work out your answer before reading on. The answer is thirty thousand dollars, the one-person minimum. If two pedestrians had been hurt, the two-or-more-people minimum of sixty thousand dollars would apply. If the crash had also damaged a parked car, the twenty-five-thousand-dollar property minimum would cover that part. Remember that the driver must also hand proof of insurance to the officer and to anyone involved who asks for it.

lines.text: Show proof routinely and on demand.

narration.text: Let us sum up. The Safety Responsibility Act makes every owner and operator financially answerable for death, injury, or property damage they cause, with at least minimum liability insurance required. The minimums are thirty thousand dollars for one person, sixty thousand for two or more people, and twenty-five thousand for property. Keep insurance or qualify as self-insured, show proof routinely at licensing, registration, and inspection, and hand it to officers or crash counterparts on request. Next, we look at the different documents that count as proof of coverage.

why_how.text: Texas accepts several kinds of proof so that drivers and large vehicle owners can each show they can pay for harm caused.
Deposits and certificates let some owners prove responsibility without a standard policy.

scenario.text: A delivery company owns thirty vehicles and wants to prove financial responsibility without buying a policy for each one.

reasoning.text: Owners of more than twenty-five vehicles may use a DPS self-insurance certificate.

result.text: With thirty vehicles, the company qualifies for a DPS self-insurance certificate.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing the fifty-five-thousand-dollar deposit is what lets an owner self-insure.

correction.text: The deposit backs the comptroller and county-judge certificates; self-insurance depends on owning more than twenty-five vehicles.

prompt.text: A family owns two cars. Can they use a DPS self-insurance certificate as proof?

answer.text: No. Self-insurance is for owners of more than twenty-five vehicles.

rationale.text: The self-insurance certificate needs more than twenty-five vehicles; the family would use a policy or another accepted proof.

narration.text: This lesson lists the documents that count as proof of financial responsibility. Most drivers use an insurance policy and the proof form that comes with it, but Texas also accepts other kinds of proof, including money deposits, surety bonds, and self-insurance certificates for large vehicle owners. Knowing the accepted forms matters because you will be asked for proof at licensing, registration, inspection, and on the road. We will split the list into two groups, proof that comes from an insurance company and proof that comes from deposits or certificates, and then compare the numbers.

The most common proof starts with an insurance policy that meets the minimum limits. Texas also accepts a standard insurance-department proof form. That form names the insurer, the policy number and policy period, each insured party, the limits or a statement that the policy complies, and the make and model of each covered vehicle. A compliance-showing insurance binder is accepted as well. The binder must show that the coverage complies. Each of these comes from an insurance company and shows the policy meets Texas requirements.

Other proof does not come from a standard policy. A comptroller certificate shows a deposit of fifty-five thousand dollars in money or securities. A surety bond can be filed with DPS. A county-judge certificate shows a deposit of fifty-five thousand dollars in cash or a cashier's check. Finally, owners of more than twenty-five vehicles may hold a DPS self-insurance certificate. Each one is a recognized alternative to a standard policy. For most new drivers, a policy and its proof form are the simplest way to meet the requirement every time proof is requested.

Here is a trap built from two numbers in the proof list. Both the comptroller certificate and the county-judge certificate rest on a deposit of fifty-five thousand dollars. Self-insurance is different. It does not depend on a deposit amount in the handbook; it depends on owning more than twenty-five vehicles. Learners sometimes swap the two, thinking a large deposit lets anyone self-insure, or that twenty-five thousand is a deposit amount. When a question mentions a deposit, think fifty-five thousand. When it mentions self-insurance, think of the fleet size, more than twenty-five vehicles.

Here is a quick check: a family owns two cars and asks whether they can use a DPS self-insurance certificate as their proof. Work out your answer before reading on. No, they cannot. The self-insurance certificate is only for owners of more than twenty-five vehicles. The family would instead use a minimum-limits policy with the standard proof form or a binder, or one of the deposit or bond options. For most families, a policy is the practical choice, and the standard proof form names the insurer, policy number, period, insured parties, limits, and covered vehicles.

To wrap up, accepted proof starts with a minimum-limits policy, the standard insurance-department proof form listing the insurer, policy number and period, insured parties, limits or a compliance statement, and each covered vehicle, or a compliance-showing binder. Other proof includes a comptroller certificate over a fifty-five-thousand-dollar deposit of money or securities, a DPS surety bond, a county-judge certificate over a fifty-five-thousand-dollar cash or cashier's check deposit, or a DPS self-insurance certificate for owners of more than twenty-five vehicles. Next, what happens when proof is missing.

why_how.text: Penalties for driving without proof grow with each conviction so that repeat uninsured driving becomes very costly.
A citation can be dismissed when coverage existed, so drivers who were insured are not punished for a missing card.

scenario.text: Omar is stopped and cannot find his proof card, though his policy was active.

reasoning.text: Missing proof draws a citation, but courts may dismiss it when a policy covered the citation moment.

result.text: Omar brings proof that his policy was in force, and the court may dismiss the citation.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a first conviction without proof already brings impoundment and suspension.

correction.text: A first conviction ends in a fine alone; suspension, bigger fines, and impoundment come with later convictions.

prompt.text: A driver is convicted a second time of driving without sufficient proof. What can happen to the vehicle?

answer.text: It can be impounded for one hundred eighty days if the driver owns it.

rationale.text: Second and later convictions add suspension, fines of three hundred fifty to one thousand dollars, and a one-hundred-eighty-day impoundment.

narration.text: This lesson covers what happens when a driver cannot show proof of insurance. First, there is good news: an image on your phone can count as proof if it shows the right facts. Then we look at the citation a driver gets without proof, how a court can dismiss it when coverage really existed, and the penalties that follow a conviction without coverage. Those penalties start with a fine and grow sharply with later convictions. Paying attention to the order of the penalties will help you answer questions that describe a first or a repeat conviction.

lines.text: Covered at the time: dismissal possible.

narration.text: An image on a phone or other wireless device counts as proof of coverage if it carries the same facts as the standard proof form. If you cannot show any proof, you get a citation. But courts may dismiss that citation when a policy actually covered you at the moment you were cited. So the citation is about missing proof, while the real question is whether you had coverage. If you did, bring that proof to court. If you did not, the case can end in a conviction, and the penalties we cover next apply, starting with a fine on a first conviction.

lines.text: First: fine of one seventy-five to three fifty.
Owner-driven vehicle impounded one eighty days.

narration.text: A conviction for driving without sufficient proof brings a fine of one hundred seventy-five to three hundred fifty dollars the first time. After that, later convictions suspend the license, bring fines of three hundred fifty to one thousand dollars, and allow the court to impound a vehicle the driver owns for one hundred eighty days. Before that vehicle is released, proof of insurance must be shown. So the penalties climb fast. A first conviction is costly, and each later conviction can take away both your license and your car for months, which makes keeping coverage the cheapest choice.

Here is a trap built from the penalty steps. Learners often think a first conviction already brings suspension and impoundment. It does not. A first conviction ends in a fine alone, from one hundred seventy-five to three hundred fifty dollars. Second and later convictions add a license suspension, bigger fines of three hundred fifty to one thousand dollars, and a one-hundred-eighty-day impoundment of a vehicle the driver owns. A second trap is mixing up a citation and a conviction. A citation can be dismissed if coverage existed; a conviction means coverage was missing.

Here is a quick check: a driver is convicted a second time of driving without sufficient proof of insurance. What can happen to a vehicle that driver owns? Work out your answer before reading on. The court can impound it for one hundred eighty days, and proof of insurance must be shown before it is released. The driver also faces a license suspension and a fine of three hundred fifty to one thousand dollars. Had this been a first conviction, the result would have been a fine alone, from one hundred seventy-five to three hundred fifty dollars.

Let us sum up. A phone image carrying the standard-form facts proves coverage. Missing proof draws a citation, and a court may dismiss it when a policy covered you at that moment. A first conviction without sufficient proof brings a fine of one hundred seventy-five to three hundred fifty dollars. Later convictions suspend the license, raise fines to three hundred fifty to one thousand dollars, and allow a one-hundred-eighty-day impoundment of an owner-driven vehicle, with proof due before release. Next, the suspensions that follow uninsured crashes and unpaid judgments.

why_how.text: Suspension pushes uninsured drivers to prove coverage and pay crash victims before they drive again.
Keeping proof for two years after a conviction shows a driver has stayed insured.

scenario.text: Grace, uninsured, causes a crash that does two thousand dollars of property damage, and a judgment against her looks likely.

reasoning.text: An uninsured crash with one thousand dollars or more of property damage and a likely judgment triggers suspension.

result.text: Grace faces suspension, and if a judgment is entered she must satisfy it within sixty days.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking proof only has to be kept for sixty days after a suspension.

correction.text: Sixty days is the window to satisfy a crash judgment; proof must be kept two years from the latest conviction.

memory_support.text: Sixty to pay, two years to prove.

prompt.text: A driver has an unpaid crash judgment. How long before it leads to suspension?

rationale.text: An unpaid crash judgment past sixty days suspends registration, license, or privilege; proof is then kept two years from the latest conviction.

narration.text: This final lesson in the section explains when Texas suspends a driver's registration, license, or driving privilege under the financial responsibility rules. Some triggers follow a conviction without proof. Others follow a crash, either an unpaid judgment or a serious crash with no insurance. You will also learn how long proof must be kept after these events and where to find more detailed guidance. Several time periods appear here, sixty days and two years, and they describe different things, so the goal is to match each period to the right duty before we move on to right of way.

title.text: Triggers tied to proof and judgments

lines.text: Suspendable conviction without proof to DPS.
Unpaid crash judgment past sixty days.

narration.text: Your registration, license, or driving privilege can be suspended in several situations. One is a conviction for a suspendable traffic offense when you have not given DPS proof of insurance. Another is an unpaid crash judgment that goes past sixty days. A third is defaulting on an installment agreement you made to pay for crash damages. Each of these shows a driver who caused harm or broke a law without showing they can pay. Note that the suspension can reach your vehicle registration as well as your license, so both the car and the driver can be taken off the road.

title.text: Uninsured crashes and the proof period

lines.text: Death, injury, or a thousand dollars damage.
Keep proof two years after conviction.

narration.text: Suspension also follows an uninsured crash that kills or injures someone or causes at least one thousand dollars of property damage, when a judgment against the driver looks likely. After these events, proof of insurance must be maintained for two years from the latest conviction date. For more detail, the handbook points to the DPS financial-responsibility pages and to the Enforcement and Compliance Service in Austin. Those are the places to look if you face one of these situations, because they explain the steps for clearing a suspension and filing the proof that is required.

lines.text: One thousand dollars of property damage.
A likely judgment against the driver.

narration.text: Look closely at what makes an uninsured crash serious enough for suspension review. It must involve a death, an injury, or at least one thousand dollars of property damage, and a judgment against the driver must look likely. If none of these results occurs, or no judgment looks likely, this trigger does not apply. This is another reason to keep coverage at all times. With insurance, the policy answers for the harm. Without it, a single crash that crosses one of these lines can put the driver's license and registration at risk.

lines.text: Crash judgment: satisfy within sixty days.
Proof: keep two years after conviction.

narration.text: Here is a trap built from two time periods. Sixty days is the window to satisfy a crash judgment. If a judgment goes unpaid past sixty days, suspension follows. Two years is how long proof of insurance must be maintained, counted from the latest conviction date. Learners sometimes think proof only matters for sixty days, or that a judgment can wait two years. Neither is right. If a question is about paying a judgment, think sixty days. If it is about keeping proof of insurance afterward, think two years from the latest conviction.

Here is a quick check: a driver has a crash judgment against them and has not paid it. How long can it go unpaid before it leads to suspension? Work out your answer before reading on. The answer is sixty days. After that, the driver's registration, license, or privilege can be suspended. Once suspended under these rules, the driver must maintain proof of insurance for two years from the latest conviction date. A defaulted installment agreement for crash damages can also lead to suspension, so keeping up with payments matters too.

lines.text: No proof or unpaid judgment suspends.

narration.text: To wrap up, registration, license, or privilege can be suspended after a suspendable conviction without insurance proof to DPS, an unpaid crash judgment past sixty days, or a defaulted crash installment agreement. Suspension also follows an uninsured crash that kills, injures, or causes one thousand dollars of property damage when a judgment looks likely. Proof must be maintained two years from the latest conviction date. More guidance is on the DPS financial-responsibility pages and with the Enforcement and Compliance Service in Austin. That completes the safety responsibility section.
